bullets.text: Risk-on: leaning into risky assets, 9th night in a row, VIX calm at 14.9.
Your book holds 7 positions, heat comfortable at 1.0%.
CAPR is flagged tonight and worth a look.

regime.title: Regime
regime.note: Is money flowing toward risk or away from it? Tonight's read on the market's mood.

about.heading: What decides it
about.body: Three inputs move the label: the VIX, its term structure, and high-yield credit spreads. The other seven inputs are tracked and shown but do not vote.

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: “Risk-on” means money is flowing toward risk; the VIX is a fear gauge (lower is calmer). Open the drivers to see which inputs argued which way.

regime-timeline.title: Regime timeline
regime-timeline.note: How the market's mood has shifted across recent nights.

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: Each dot is one nightly snapshot; higher means more fear (the VIX). Color is that night's verdict: green risk-on, red risk-off, amber mixed.

about.heading: Why it matters
about.body: A mood that just flipped is weaker evidence than one that has held for weeks; watch the streak rather than any single night.

macro-drivers.title: Macro drivers
macro-drivers.note: The three inputs that actually decide the regime call, with their recent history.

about.heading: What they are
about.body: The 10y–2y Treasury spread (the recession watcher), the high-yield credit spread (are lenders scared?), and the VIX (the equity fear gauge).

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: Each tile shows today's value, the one-day change, and the last 90 observations' trend.

candidates.title: Research candidates
candidates.note: A reading queue of good companies whose shares are currently marked down; nothing on it is a recommendation.

about.heading: What this screens for
about.body: Quality first: durable returns on capital, real free cash flow, a rising Piotroski score, and a share price currently well off its highs.

about.heading: How it differs from the scorecard
about.body: The scorecard below finds stocks doing something odd right now; this finds good businesses that happen to be cheap. Quality enters the funnel here; dislocation is only the timing.

about.heading: What happens next
about.body: Names go to deep research before any decision. List entries are graded for calibration only — see Candidates screen edge under Track record.

research-reopens.title: Research reopens
research-reopens.note: Researched names set aside, each with the evidence that would reopen the question.

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: A dated trigger is usually an earnings report; “due” means that evidence now exists and the name deserves a fresh look. An event trigger waits on a filing or a price, with no date attached.

about.heading: Lifecycle
about.body: A row retires when the name is re-researched; the ticker links to the full thesis.

scorecard.title: Ticker scorecard
scorecard.note: Stocks doing something statistically odd right now, which says nothing about business quality.

about.heading: What this is
about.body: Every signal here is market microstructure — short interest, days-to-cover, oversold RSI, FTD spikes, retail chatter. A high score means something unusual is happening to the stock, usually a small one, and says nothing about the business.

about.heading: Why a crashing stock flags bullish
about.body: Deeply oversold RSI and crowded shorts vote bullish on a mean-reversion hunch. That hunch is worthless when the drop had a real cause: a stock down 40% on bad news will sit here flagged bullish every night until the price stabilizes.

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: The bar is the summed vote, left of center bearish; Split is the raw bullish/bearish count; ★ marks strong agreement.

about.heading: How much to trust it
about.body: Treat it as a to-research feed: most flags deserve rejection, and by design the research step kills nearly everything. Whether any single signal has proven edge is graded under Track record; so far none has.

signal-efficacy.title: Signal efficacy
signal-efficacy.note: Every signal's raw report card against simply holding SPY.

about.heading: What this is
about.body: How often each signal has been right so far, and by how much it beat the SPY benchmark. Unfiltered: every signal appears, proven or not.

about.heading: Where the verdict lives
about.body: Whether a signal is trustworthy yet is decided in Signal recommendations below, which grades against the real base rate instead of a coin flip.

signal-efficacy.caveat: Small sample; windows overlap, so one hot week can flatter several signals at once. Grades firm up as distinct composite dates accumulate.
signal-efficacy.empty: no matured signal outcomes yet; appears once a signal's flagged calls reach their grading horizon

bucket-performance.title: Bucket performance
bucket-performance.note: Did stronger conviction actually produce better forward returns?

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: Every past opinion grouped by conviction bucket, strong-bull down to strong-bear, each graded against SPY. If conviction means anything, stronger buckets should do better; this checks that.

bucket-performance.caveat: Buckets group flags by strength, not by independence; the same overlapping-episode caveat applies within each bucket. Read the count before trusting a bucket's average.
bucket-performance.empty: no matured buckets yet; appears once conviction-bucketed opinions reach their grading horizon

human-filter.title: Human-filter tally
human-filter.note: When you chose which flags to act on and which to pass, did your judgment add anything?

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: Compares forward returns of the opinions you acted on versus the ones you passed. The gap between the two is the value of the human filter.

human-filter.caveat: Compares acted-on vs. passed-on flags from a still-small decision journal. A handful of trades can swing the comparison either way.
human-filter.empty: no matured flagged opinions yet; appears once an acted-on or passed-on flag reaches its grading horizon

regime-performance.title: Regime edge
regime-performance.note: Does the market-mood call itself predict forward returns?

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: Each row is one mood at one horizon: did risk-on nights actually precede better returns than risk-off nights?

regime-performance.caveat: Regime windows are contiguous stretches rather than independent draws; a single risk-on run dominates the sample until more regimes accumulate.
regime-performance.empty: no matured regime outcomes yet — appears once a market-mood window reaches its grading horizon

pending.title: In-flight opinions
pending.note: Opinions recorded but not yet old enough to grade.

about.heading: What this is
about.body: Every graded table above includes only matured outcomes. This is the queue still being measured; these rows become those grades once they age.

pending.caveat: These flags haven't reached their grading horizon yet, so nothing here is a result; it's a worklist.
pending.empty: nothing pending (everything registered so far has matured); fills once tonight's opinions are registered

basis-breaks.title: Data-integrity checks
basis-breaks.note: Price moves that look like data errors, caught before they can poison the grades; an empty table is the good outcome.

about.heading: What this is
about.body: Days where a price moved so far it looks like a stock split or a bad tick rather than a real move. Surfaced so a silent data problem cannot quietly skew every grade above.

basis-breaks.empty: no basis breaks detected, which is the good outcome; fills only when a price move looks like a split or a bad tick

book-heat.title: Advisor book heat
book-heat.note: How much of your account is genuinely at risk right now.

about.heading: What “heat” means
about.body: The dollars lost across every open position on a one-ATR adverse day: a normal bad day, not a crash.

about.heading: What it is not
about.body: Not the stop-out loss: stops sit further out, so being stopped costs more. Coverage says how much of the book the number actually accounts for — positions missing inputs count as uncovered.

group-heat.title: Advisor group heat
group-heat.note: Correlated positions collapsed into single bets.

about.heading: Why
about.body: Two energy names are one energy bet: risk adds up within a group, and sizing that ignores this quietly doubles exposure. Hedges net out, so a protective put reduces its bet's heat.

group-heat.empty: no group heat yet; appears once the advisor computes tonight's book

position-heat.title: Per-position heat
position-heat.note: Each holding's contribution to the risk totals above.

about.heading: What “heat” means
about.body: Quantity × ATR: the dollars at risk on a one-ATR adverse day, not the loss if the stop triggers. The detail behind the book and group totals.

disagreements.title: Disagreements
disagreements.note: Positions you hold that tonight's signals argue against.

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: Tickers where the score points the opposite way from an open position. “Strong” means the score is far enough from neutral to be worth a look. Treat it as a prompt to re-check the thesis rather than an exit order.

size-caps.title: Size caps
size-caps.note: A volatility-scaled ceiling on each candidate's size; the advisor only suggests, it never places orders.

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: More volatile names get smaller ceilings, so a one-ATR bad day costs roughly the same dollars across positions. The warning marker means the cap exceeds current buying power.

plan-001-report.title: Signal recommendations
plan-001-report.note: The verdict on each signal (keep, watch, or anti-signal), graded against the real base rate.

about.heading: Why the base rate matters
about.body: A randomly chosen scored ticker beat its benchmark only ~40% of the time over these windows, so a 61% hit-rate can still be worth nothing. Every verdict is measured against that baseline, not a coin flip.

about.heading: The verdicts
about.body: “Keep” means the whole confidence range sits above the baseline; “anti-signal” sits entirely below it (significantly wrong, never a win); “watch” straddles.

about.heading: Hold it loosely
about.body: Several signals are graded at once, so a few clear the bar by luck. Re-weighting the catalog is always a human decision; nothing here feeds back automatically.

plan-001-report.caveat: A backtest replay against ALFRED vintages, not live trading. Read excess and beats-baseline rather than hit-rate alone, and remember this is one history, not a distribution.
plan-001-report.empty: insufficient evidence for every signal so far, which is expected of a young scorer; fills in once a signal's evidence crosses the reliability floor

plan-004-scorecard.title: Trader scorecard
plan-004-scorecard.note: A grade of your past decision quality.

about.heading: What this is
about.body: A plain-text report: did filtering the flags help, what did execution cost, and how did unrecommended (freelance) trades do?

text_lines: Filter edge (acted vs passed, by horizon)
coverage: 19 ledger dates 2026-07-05..2026-08-07, 7 trading days missing
plan-004-scorecard.caveat: Grades the human's own decisions from the journal. Coverage is whatever got journaled, not a random sample of every flag shown.

candidate-efficacy.title: Candidates screen edge
candidate-efficacy.note: Does the candidates screen's timing beat SPY after a name first enters the list?

about.heading: How it is measured
about.body: A name's first entry onto the reading list starts a stopwatch: its 21- and 63-trading-day return is measured against SPY, split by which dislocation door let it in (oversold RSI, a price drawdown, or both at once).

about.heading: What it does not grade
about.body: Timing only, never the multi-year quality thesis behind the pick, and none of it feeds back into the screen's own gates.

candidate-efficacy.caveat: Episodes are few and overlap early. The view carries plain averages with no confidence interval, so read n before believing any row.
candidate-efficacy.empty: no matured episodes yet; first grades appear ~21 trading days after the first screen night

health.title: Pipeline health
health.note: Did last night's machinery actually run, and is every database fresh?

about.heading: What it checks
about.body: Three layers: every scheduled job's last exit code and whether any is hung mid-run, FAILED/STALE markers in the last 24h of logs (as counts; the log itself stays on the host), and each database's newest snapshot age against its expected cadence.

about.heading: How to read it
about.body: Green with zero problems is the normal state. Any row here means a number elsewhere on this page may be stale, so check this section first when something looks off.

glossary.Screener: one of the small programs here that visits a single official data source and files away what it finds. There are about seventeen, one per source.
glossary.Monitor: like a screener, but instead of measuring today it keeps a calendar of upcoming events: central-bank meetings, company earnings dates, market holidays.
glossary.Combiner: a program that reads what the screeners and monitors collected and derives something from it: an overall market opinion, a stock scorecard, a report card on past opinions. Combiners never fetch anything from the internet.
glossary.Market regime: a one-line summary of the market's overall mood (roughly: calm, nervous, or stressed), distilled from many indicators at once.
glossary.Z-score: a way of saying "how unusual is today's number compared with its own history?" Zero means perfectly typical; +2 or −2 means rare. Used here to spot readings worth a second look.
glossary.Short interest: how many of a company's shares investors have borrowed and sold, betting the price will fall. High short interest means many people are betting against the stock.
glossary.Fails-to-deliver: trades where the seller didn't hand over the shares on time. Occasional fails are plumbing noise; persistent ones can hint at stress or heavy short-selling in a stock.
glossary.FTD: trades where the seller didn't hand over the shares on time. Occasional fails are plumbing noise; persistent ones can hint at stress or heavy short-selling in a stock.
glossary.Dark pool: a private marketplace where large investors trade shares away from the public exchanges. The trades are real and eventually reported; "dark" refers to the order book not being publicly visible.
glossary.ATS: a private marketplace where large investors trade shares away from the public exchanges. The trades are real and eventually reported; "dark" refers to the order book not being publicly visible.
glossary.Put/call ratio: compares the volume of bets that prices will fall (puts) against bets that they'll rise (calls). An unusually high ratio suggests widespread nervousness.
glossary.VIX: a widely quoted index of how much turbulence traders expect over the next month, often called the market's "fear gauge." Low ≈ complacent; high ≈ frightened.
glossary.OPEX: options-expiration day, when a large batch of options contracts expires at once (typically the third Friday of the month). Markets can behave oddly around it, so the calendar here tracks it.
glossary.Yield curve: the pattern of interest rates on government debt from short loans to long ones. Normally longer loans pay more; when the curve "inverts" (short rates above long rates), it has historically preceded recessions.
glossary.COT / positioning: the Commitments of Traders report, a weekly government publication showing what large professional traders are betting in futures markets. Extreme positioning can mark crowded trades.
glossary.Backtest: replaying the system's rules against past data to see how they *would* have done — using only the information that was actually available on each historical day, so the replay can't cheat by peeking at the future.
glossary.Forward return: how a stock actually performed in the weeks *after* the system flagged it. "Paper" means graded on the record only; no money moved.
glossary.paper outcome: how a stock actually performed in the weeks *after* the system flagged it. "Paper" means graded on the record only; no money moved.
glossary.Settings UI: `uv run python config_ui.py`; a local browser page that edits `.env` (the file holding your keys and tuning knobs) safely, with API keys shown masked.
glossary.ATR: a measure of how much a stock typically bounces around in a single day. Higher ATR means more volatility; used here to size positions—bigger ATR, smaller bet.
glossary.average true range: a measure of how much a stock typically bounces around in a single day. Higher ATR means more volatility; used here to size positions—bigger ATR, smaller bet.
glossary.Book heat / Heat: a summary of how much money is riding on your current holdings, adjusted for market swings. High heat means concentrated risk; useful for knowing whether the portfolio is humming quietly or wearing thin.
glossary.Coverage: how much of the full picture actually has data behind it. On the ticker scorecard it's the share of the signals that could have had an opinion on a stock tonight that actually did — low coverage means the score rests on just a few inputs, not the whole roster. On the book-heat panel it's the share of your holdings' value where a real risk read (an ATR) was available to size it — low coverage means the heat number is missing pieces of the book.
glossary.Hit rate: in the backtester's report, the percentage of time the system's opinion was right (price went the way it was flagged). Always read alongside the benchmarks—if prices drift up anyway, a bearish flag "wins" by doing nothing.
glossary.Confidence interval: a range around a measured result that's probably correct, expressed as "the true answer is here about 95% of the time." A wide interval means less certainty; a narrow one means more.
glossary.CI: a range around a measured result that's probably correct, expressed as "the true answer is here about 95% of the time." A wide interval means less certainty; a narrow one means more.
glossary.Piotroski score: a simple nine-factor check of a company's financial health, ranging from 0 (weak) to 9 (strong). Looks at profitability, asset quality, and cash flow—rough, but a useful beginning-of-funnel filter.
glossary.Risk-on / risk-off: the market's mood in broad strokes. "Risk-on" means investors are buying stocks and taking chances; "risk-off" means they're retreating to safe havens like bonds and cash.
glossary.Score: the nightly sum of a ticker's signal votes. Positive means more bullish signals fired than bearish ones. The size says how lopsided the vote was, not how far the price will move.
glossary.composite score: the nightly sum of a ticker's signal votes. Positive means more bullish signals fired than bearish ones. The size says how lopsided the vote was, not how far the price will move.
glossary.Base rate: how often the benchmark moved that way anyway. A hit rate only means something when it beats this number; otherwise the "wins" were just the market drifting.
glossary.Edge: hit rate minus base rate. A positive edge means the signal called direction better than the market's own drift; zero means it added nothing.
glossary.Excess: how much better or worse a stock did than the benchmark over the same stretch. Positive excess means it beat the market, not just that it went up.
glossary.excess return: how much better or worse a stock did than the benchmark over the same stretch. Positive excess means it beat the market, not just that it went up.
glossary.Directional excess: excess return counted in the direction the signal called. A bearish flag earns positive directional excess when the stock does *worse* than the market.
glossary.RSI: a 0-to-100 gauge of how hard a stock has been bought or sold lately. Below about 30 usually reads as oversold; above 70, overbought.
glossary.relative strength index: a 0-to-100 gauge of how hard a stock has been bought or sold lately. Below about 30 usually reads as oversold; above 70, overbought.
glossary.ROIC: how much profit a company earns on each dollar tied up in the business. A steady double-digit ROIC is a mark of quality.
glossary.return on invested capital: how much profit a company earns on each dollar tied up in the business. A steady double-digit ROIC is a mark of quality.
glossary.FCF yield: the spare cash a business generates in a year, divided by the stock-market value of its shares (market cap). Higher means each dollar of cash costs you less to own.
glossary.free cash flow yield: the spare cash a business generates in a year, divided by the stock-market value of its shares (market cap). Higher means each dollar of cash costs you less to own.
glossary.Market cap: the total price tag on all of a company's shares put together.
glossary.market capitalization: the total price tag on all of a company's shares put together.
glossary.Reverse DCF: instead of guessing what a stock is worth, hold the cash-flow assumptions fixed and solve for the yearly return today's price already bakes in. A high implied return on cautious assumptions is interesting; a low one on rosy assumptions is a warning.
glossary.implied return: instead of guessing what a stock is worth, hold the cash-flow assumptions fixed and solve for the yearly return today's price already bakes in. A high implied return on cautious assumptions is interesting; a low one on rosy assumptions is a warning.
glossary.Hurdle: the return an investment has to beat to be worth the risk: the safe Treasury rate plus a premium scaled by beta — the stock's exposure to market-wide swings, not its own choppiness. An implied return only means something next to this number.
glossary.cost of equity: the return an investment has to beat to be worth the risk: the safe Treasury rate plus a premium scaled by beta — the stock's exposure to market-wide swings, not its own choppiness. An implied return only means something next to this number.
glossary.Equity risk premium: the extra yearly return investors demand for holding stocks instead of Treasuries. Damodaran re-solves it monthly from the market's own level; it is the market-wide half of the hurdle.
glossary.ERP: the extra yearly return investors demand for holding stocks instead of Treasuries. Damodaran re-solves it monthly from the market's own level; it is the market-wide half of the hurdle.
glossary.Terminal value: the part of a valuation covering everything past the forecast years, usually most of the total. It leans on a "forever" growth rate, which is why that one assumption gets policed hardest.
glossary.Terminal growth: the forever growth rate inside the terminal value. Capped at the Treasury rate (nothing outgrows the economy forever), and real growth above inflation has to be paid for with reinvested earnings.
glossary.Enterprise value: the market value of a company's equity and debt together, net of its cash: what buying the whole business would cost, not just its shares.
glossary.EV: the market value of a company's equity and debt together, net of its cash: what buying the whole business would cost, not just its shares.
glossary.Beta: a stock's exposure to risk that diversification can't remove: how much it moves with the market, standardized around 1. Not the same as volatility — a wild mover that ignores the market can still have a low beta.
glossary.Reinvestment rate: the share of profit plowed back into the business instead of flowing out as free cash. Growth has to be paid from here: growth rate = reinvestment rate × return on that reinvested capital.
glossary.Data age: how many days old the freshest input behind a number is. Small means current; large means the reading is running on stale data.
